summary:
Twenty-five verses from "a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James" — and since the James best known by that bare name led the Jerusalem church and was a brother of Jesus, Jude has traditionally been counted a brother of Jesus as well. He tells his readers he had planned a different letter, about the salvation they share, but changed course on urgent news: intruders had "crept in unnoticed," turning God's grace into a license for immorality. The letter's purpose is in verse 3: "contend earnestly for the faith entrusted once for all to the saints."

Jude's method is distinctive. He argues almost entirely by example, stacking up figures of judgment: the unbelieving wilderness generation, the angels who fell, Sodom, Cain, Balaam, Korah. And he reaches beyond the Hebrew canon to books his audience knew well: the archangel Michael disputing with the devil over the body of Moses (a story from a Jewish work known as the Assumption of Moses) and a direct quotation from 1 Enoch, an apocalyptic book widely read in the Judaism of the period. The imagery for the intruders piles up the same way — clouds without rain, fruitless trees twice dead, wild waves foaming up their shame, wandering stars.

Then the letter turns. After all the warning, it closes with one of the New Testament's best-loved benedictions: "Now to Him who is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you unblemished in His glorious presence, with great joy" (vv. 24-25). Notice where the confidence rests: not in the community's vigilance, though Jude demands it, but in the God who keeps them from falling.
